post.originalText:
A quantum puppy splits into 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 copies, tunnels through a wall, and fetches one tennis ball.

Studios quote $1,000 to $5,000 for a single minute of animated science explainer. Science YouTubers, edtech startups, and online courses need one every week. Most just skip the animation.

The media thought that was the story. It was not.

The clip was made by Claude Opus 5.5 in 24 seconds. The model draws with code: it writes the animation as a program, renders it, looks at the output, and edits the file. According to https://t.co/ySIqJbuAzG and https://t.co/JiGCQRDevN, that closed-loop pipeline is why Opus handles short animations now. Not a new artistic modality. Elite agentic coding plus visual feedback.

The barrier was never animation skill. It was the motion studio invoice, the render worker, the project manager, and the four-week timeline. One prompt now collapses all of it into a code file you can edit like any other.

The economics break in a specific place. A physics teacher who already owns the subscription can now produce the explainer the department budget couldn't cover. Not cheaper animation. Zero-marginal-cost animation for anyone with an API key.

Polymarket prices 'Will Anthropic IPO by December 31, 2026?' at 72% and 'Will Anthropic's initial public offering occur in November 2026?' at 55%. The market is betting on an IPO timeline, but the real story is that the product capability is already outrunning any institutional roadmap. The bypass happened at the individual level, and the consensus hasn't noticed.
